topic: Binary Logic in the Towers of Hanoi
target_audience: High school students interested in computer science and discrete mathematics

outline.topic: Binary Logic in the Towers of Hanoi
outline.target_audience: High school students interested in computer science and discrete mathematics

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Nature of Binary
sections.content: Briefly introduce the binary system as a base-2 counting method (0 and 1). Explain that each bit represents a power of 2, mirroring the structure of branching decisions.

sections.title: Mapping Towers of Hanoi to Binary
sections.content: Introduce the puzzle: moving n disks from Peg A to Peg C using Peg B. Explain that the sequence of moves corresponds directly to the binary counting sequence (001, 010, 011, etc.).
sections.example: For 3 disks, the total moves = 2^3 - 1 = 7. Each move corresponds to an integer from 1 to 7 represented in 3 bits.

sections.title: The Disk-Movement Rule
sections.content: Explain the elegant link: The disk that moves at step 'i' is determined by the position of the rightmost '1' in the binary representation of 'i'.
sections.example: In a 3-disk puzzle, at step 4 (Binary 100), the 3rd disk moves because the rightmost '1' is in the 3rd position.

sections.title: Visualizing the Algorithm
sections.content: Show an animation of a monk (The Algorithm) moving disks based on the binary state. The binary bits 'toggle' as the monk completes each move, showing the cyclical nature of the puzzle.
sections.example: A 3-disk stack shifting: Step 1 (001) -> Move smallest disk. Step 2 (010) -> Move second smallest. Step 3 (011) -> Move smallest disk again.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.content: Reinforce that the Towers of Hanoi is not just a game, but a physical manifestation of a binary counter. This highlights how complex recursive problems can be solved through simple binary logic.
sections.example: Summary table: Disks (n) vs Binary sequence length (2^n - 1), demonstrating exponential growth in steps required.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Nature of Binary
lecture_lines: Binary uses only digits zero and one.
Each position represents a power of two.
Counting in binary follows a simple pattern.
animations: Display binary number 000 in #FFFFFF color at center.
Animate 000 changing to 001, highlighting last digit in #FF4500.
Show 010, highlighting second digit with #FF4500 color.
Show 011, highlighting last two digits in #FF4500.
Display 100, highlighting first digit in #FF4500 color.

storyboard.title: Mapping Towers of Hanoi to Binary
lecture_lines: Towers of Hanoi puzzles have specific moves.
Binary counting maps directly to these moves.
Three disks take seven total moves.
animations: Display three pegs labeled Peg A, B, C (#FFFFFF).
Add 3 disks on Peg A, using #1E90FF color.
Highlight disk 1 as '1' (binary), disk 2 as '2', etc.

storyboard.title: The Disk-Movement Rule
lecture_lines: The disk moving depends on step number.
Look for the rightmost one in binary.
Position of one determines disk size.
animations: Draw three disks on Peg A using #40E0D0 color.
Show disk 1 moving from Peg A to Peg C.
Show arrow indicator (#FFFF00) pointing to disk 1.

storyboard.title: Visualizing the Algorithm
lecture_lines: Binary bits toggle as moves occur.
This process reveals a recursive structure.
animations: Display recursion tree structure in #D3D3D3 color.
Highlight left branch (#FF6347) for moving n-1 disks.
Highlight right branch (#32CD32) for moving nth disk.

storyboard.title: Summary and Conclusion
lecture_lines: Towers of Hanoi reflects binary counting.
Recursive problems often have binary solutions.
Complexity arises from simple binary rules.
animations: Show text 'Hanoi = Binary' in #FFA500 at center.
Fade in summary points 1 to 3 in #FFFFFF.
Highlight the complete link between steps and binary.
